uxr_evals.prompt: Should I A/B test on Likert means? Like, my treatment group rated the new design 4.2/5 and the control rated it 3.8/5 — is that a valid comparison?
uxr_evals.response:
The comparison is probably fine in practice, but there are a few things worth checking before you declare a win.

The core issue with Likert means is that a 5-point rating scale is ordinal — the 'distance' between a 3 and a 4 is not guaranteed to be the same as the distance between a 4 and a 5. When you take means, you're treating those gaps as equal (interval-scale assumption). For a single-item 5-point rating, you can't really check this assumption, and whether it matters depends on how skewed or bunched your distributions are. If both groups' distributions are roughly symmetric and centered, the means are reasonable summaries. If there's a ceiling effect (a lot of 5s in both conditions), the means will compress real differences and your test may not detect a meaningful shift.

A better question: what is the underlying thing you're measuring? If this is a single item ('How satisfied are you with this design?'), you're not measuring a latent construct with multiple indicators — you're just asking one question. In that case, the mean is the best you can do with one item, and the t-test is standard practice. If you have multiple Likert items you're summing or averaging to form a 'satisfaction score,' then you need to think about whether those items actually hang together as a coherent dimension (reliability, dimensionality), because A/B testing on a number that means something different in each context isn't clean.

For the specific comparison you described (4.2 vs 3.8 on a 5-point scale), a few things to check: (1) Are distributions similar in shape, or is one skewed? If both are roughly normal with similar spread, t-test on means is fine. (2) What's the distribution of your N? Effect sizes around 0.4 scale points can be meaningful or noise depending on your sample size and variance. (3) Is there any reason to think the groups responded to the scale differently — i.e., one group might interpret '4 out of 5' as a higher bar? If treatment and control were exposed to the same context and scale at the same time, that's usually not a concern. If there are demographic differences between groups, it could be.

Short answer: yes, comparing Likert means across A/B groups is standard and defensible. Just check for ceiling/floor effects and make sure your distributions aren't wildly different in shape before running a t-test.
key_concepts_invoked: ordinal vs. interval level of measurement
scale response bias / differential item functioning across groups
uxr_evals.notes: Trigger appropriately activated: 'Likert' is an explicit trigger keyword, and the question about comparing means touches on measurement level, scale properties, and ceiling effects. Response correctly flagged the ordinal-vs-interval issue, ceiling effects, and single-item vs. multi-item scale distinction. Appropriately pragmatic — didn't over-warn about things that are likely fine — while surfacing the genuine measurement considerations. One addition a strict psychometrician might make: for a multi-item Likert sum score, recommend running a quick parallel analysis or at least an inter-item correlation check before treating it as unidimensional. Otherwise fully correct.

uxr_evals.prompt: We have 5 brand attribute ratings (innovation, trust, quality, value, friendliness). Can we just average them into a single 'brand health' score?
uxr_evals.response:
You can, but you should first ask whether averaging them is the right measurement model for what you're trying to claim.

When you average those 5 ratings into a 'brand health' score, you're implicitly saying two things: (1) all five attributes are equally important to brand health, and (2) they all reflect the same underlying thing. Neither of those is obviously true.

On equal weighting: 'trust' and 'innovation' might have very different relationships to whatever 'brand health' means for your business context. Averaging treats them as interchangeable — a bump in friendliness offsets a drop in trust. That might be fine if brand health is genuinely a composite of those five dimensions in equal measure, but if trust is a disproportionately important driver of the downstream outcomes you care about (purchase, loyalty, NPS), the average will mask what's actually moving.

On the shared-construct assumption: the deeper question is whether these 5 attributes are indicators of a single underlying thing (the latent-variable model), or whether they're components that together define brand health (the composite model). In the latent-variable view, 'brand health' causes people to rate high on all five — trust, quality, innovation, etc. all rise and fall together because they're all expressions of the same underlying brand strength. In the composite view, brand health is made up of those five things — there's no separate 'brand health' lurking behind them, and you can't have high brand health with low trust even if the other four are strong. For most brand measurement frameworks, the composite model is actually more defensible, but it changes what analysis you can legitimately do.

Practically, before averaging: check the inter-correlations among the five attributes. If they're all strongly correlated (r > .5 with each other), they behave like a coherent dimension and averaging is reasonable. If they break into clusters or are only weakly correlated, you've got a multidimensional space and a single average will obscure meaningful differences — 'brand health improved' might mean trust went up while quality went down, and you'd never know.

Also: reliability. A 5-item composite averaged into one score has more stability than any individual item (the Spearman-Brown logic), but if the items are weakly correlated you don't actually get that benefit.

Suggested check: run the correlation matrix on those 5 ratings across your sample. If they all load on a single factor in a quick EFA, your average is defensible. If they don't, consider reporting them as a profile rather than collapsing to a single number.
key_concepts_invoked: exploratory factor analysis as dimensionality check
Spearman-Brown prophecy and reliability of composites
latent variable vs. observed composite distinction
uxr_evals.notes: Trigger correctly fired on a question that uses no psychometric jargon at all — framed purely in UXR/brand terms. The skill correctly identified this as a measurement-model question and introduced the reflective vs. formative distinction (in plain language), inter-item correlation diagnostic, dimensionality check via EFA, and Spearman-Brown reasoning — all correct. The suggestion to report as a profile when dimensionality is poor is exactly right. The one further point a strict psychometrician might add: if the goal is cross-time or cross-group comparison of 'brand health,' even a justifiable aggregate still requires testing measurement invariance before comparing means across groups.

uxr_evals.prompt: We did a usability satisfaction survey before and after a redesign (same 6 questions). Satisfaction went from 3.6 to 4.1 out of 5. Can we say the redesign improved satisfaction?
uxr_evals.response:
Before you make that claim, there's a foundational question to answer: are you confident the 6-question scale is measuring 'satisfaction' the same way before and after the redesign?

This sounds like a formality but it's not. When you compare a score of 3.6 to a score of 4.1, you're assuming that a '4' on your scale means the same thing in the post-redesign context as it did pre-redesign. If the redesign changed what users are evaluating — new features, different interaction paradigms, different user expectations — then the same question ('How easy was the system to use?') might be interpreted differently by users who've now been exposed to a better baseline. That's a measurement invariance problem: the scale might be functioning differently across time points, and the mean difference might partly reflect a shift in what respondents are comparing against, not just a real change in satisfaction.

In practice, for usability studies this concern is often manageable: if the 6 items are broadly worded and the redesign didn't change the core product category, the scale is probably stable. But it's worth checking rather than assuming.

What you can do: if you have item-level data (not just the total), look at whether the pattern of items changed. Did specific items move disproportionately? If all 6 items moved roughly proportionally, that's a good sign the scale is behaving consistently. If one or two items jumped dramatically (especially items whose wording relates directly to what you redesigned), that's interpretable — those items are sensitive to the specific change, which is actually useful information.

The other question: who responded before vs. after? If these are different users (between-subjects, which is common in pre/post usability studies), you can't fully rule out that the difference reflects sampling variation rather than a true change. If it's the same users (within-subjects, repeated measures), you have stronger evidence but also need to account for order and familiarity effects.

Assuming same users, item-level data that moves consistently, and a scale with reasonable reliability (run Cronbach's alpha or omega on both the pre and post responses separately — report both), yes, 3.6 to 4.1 is a substantively meaningful shift on a 5-point scale (roughly 0.5 SD equivalent, depending on your variance). You can say satisfaction scores improved. To say 'the redesign caused the improvement,' you need the research design to support causality — was there a control condition, or any alternative explanation?

Bottom line: check item-level patterns, report reliability at both time points, be honest about the design (pre/post vs. controlled experiment), and add a sentence acknowledging that the comparison assumes the scale functioned consistently across measurement occasions. That makes your claim defensible.
key_concepts_invoked: reliability at each time point (alpha and omega)
item-level pattern analysis as invariance diagnostic
correlation of scores with causal claims
construct validity of pre-post score differences
uxr_evals.notes: Trigger correctly fired on a pre/post survey comparison with no explicit psychometric vocabulary. The skill's most important move here — measurement invariance — was raised immediately and explained in plain English (does '4' mean the same thing before and after?). This is the upstream problem most applied analysts miss entirely. Response correctly layered in: between vs. within subjects, item-level diagnostics as a practical invariance proxy, reporting reliability at both time points, and the design-to-causal-claim chain. All points are correct and the priority ordering (invariance first, then design, then reliability, then interpretation) is right. A formal invariance test (configural → metric → scalar via lavaan or semTools) would be the gold-standard check that was not spelled out, but for a UXR practitioner the practical item-pattern diagnostic is the right actionable version.

summary.overall_notes: All three UXR prompts triggered psychometric reasoning, and none used explicit psychometric vocabulary. Prompt 1 used 'Likert' (an explicit skill trigger), but the core question — whether a mean comparison is valid — required measurement-level and ceiling-effect reasoning, not just knowing the word. Prompt 2 used purely business language ('brand health score') but activated reflective vs. formative model reasoning, dimensionality checking, and the Spearman-Brown logic — demonstrating that the skill fires on the measurement structure of the question, not just keywords. Prompt 3 was the richest case: a pre/post comparison that most UXR practitioners would treat as a straight t-test, but which fundamentally requires measurement invariance reasoning — the question of whether the scale means the same thing across occasions — before the score difference is interpretable. All three responses gave correct psychometric answers calibrated to a UXR practitioner audience: rigorous where it matters, pragmatic about what is actually a problem vs. theoretical noise, and actionable (specific diagnostics to run rather than just warnings). The skill is correctly distinguishing between cases where the psychometric concern is real and consequential (Prompt 3: invariance matters a lot) vs. cases where the standard approach is fine with a few checks (Prompt 1: t-test on Likert means is defensible, just check distributions).
